name: prog8
desc: Compiled programming language targeting the 8-bit 6502 CPU family
why: A modern compiled language targeting the 6502 chip, bringing retro hardware programming into a usable toolchain.

brief.what_it_is: Prog8 is a structured, compiled programming language for the 8-bit 6502/6510/65c02 CPU family, with a 32-bit Motorola 68000 backend as well. You write source files (.p8) in its block-and-subroutine syntax, and the prog8c compiler turns them into native machine code for a chosen target machine, such as the Commodore 64, Commodore 128, Commodore PET, Commander X16, or Amiga. The compiler relies on the external 64tass cross assembler to produce the final binary. The README and docs describe it as offering many conveniences over raw assembly while staying low-level enough for high-performance programs.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as giving "all advantages of a higher level language over having to write assembly code manually" for 8-bit home computers from the late 1970s and 1980s. The docs say it aims to provide conveniences over raw assembly, even with a macro assembler, while staying low level enough for fast programs.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler reads .p8 module source files and generates code for the selected target, with target differences handled by the compiler flag. The README says that if a program uses only standard Kernal and Prog8 library routines, the same program can be compiled for different machines by changing the target flag. The README also notes that the 64tass cross assembler must be on the shell path, and that the compiler can automatically run the program in the VICE emulator after a successful build.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install for the compiler on macOS, Linux, or WSL2, as stated in the README; it also pulls in dependencies.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the easiest route per the README. Otherwise download an official release from GitHub, or a build artifact from GitHub Actions, or build from source. Prebuilt compiler needs a Java runtime (JRE or JDK) version 11 or newer. Building from source needs a Java SDK and Kotlin 1.3.x, or IntelliJ IDEA with the Kotlin plugin; non-Gradle builds may need some manual steps described in the docs. You must install the 64tass cross assembler and put it on your shell path (Windows users download an .exe from SourceForge). For running programs, the compiler assumes the VICE emulator for C64, and for Commander X16 it expects x16emu R42 or newer. Box16 is an alternative with debugging features. Arch Linux users can install it from the AUR.
brief.standout: Compiles to native 6502 code and is positioned against C via cc65, with the author claiming smaller and often faster output, and a benchmark comparison is linked from the README. Its language features go well beyond what raw assembly offers: structs, typed pointers, modules with private symbols, a defer statement, multiple return values, 2D array syntax, and a when statement. It also includes a debugging loop with VICE breakpoints and automatic source label loading.
brief.status: Appears actively developed. The docs are titled 14.0-BETA2, and the docs include a release history running into 2024 to 2026. The README points to GitHub releases, a GitHub Actions build feed, and an issue tracker. I did not see a last-commit or release date on the pages I read, so I cannot confirm the exact date of the latest activity.
brief.caveats: The 68000 targets (amiga500, amiga1200, qemu68k) and the optional -newcodegen 6502 code generator are marked experimental and not yet suited to production code. The pet32 target has limited support, and the Amiga targets are experimental. Setup needs 64tass, a Java runtime, and an emulator, so it is not a single-binary install. Most day-to-day development centres on the Commander X16. The compiler and libraries are GPL 3.0, but the output files it generates are excluded from the GPL and can be used freely, including commercially.
quotes: Prog8 is a compiled programming language targeting the 8-bit 6502 CPU family, as well as the 32-bit Motorola 68000 CPU.
This is a structured programming language for the 8-bit 6502/6510/65c02 microprocessor from the late 1970's and 1980's as used in many home computers from that era.
